page_hint: Ch 15, Section 3 (Worked Example), 'Attention FLOP comparison' paragraph
quoted_clause: Attention is two matmuls per token per head — Q·K^T then ·V — each a multiply-accumulate of L²·d, so in FLOPs (2 per MAC) the per-layer cost is ≈ 4 × L² × d_model, where L=9,200 and d_model=8,192.
observed: The phrase 'per token per head' is misleading. The L²·d_h MAC count is for the full prefill of L tokens (all L queries attending to all L keys), not for a single token. For a single decode step the cost would be L·d_h (one query against L stored keys). The formula that follows (4·L²·d_model per layer) is correct for full prefill, but the 'per token' qualifier contradicts it.
evidence: Q·K^T for L queries and L keys: L×L×d_h MACs = L²·d_h. This is the cost of the entire prefill, not of one token. The text's own substitution (L=9,200) confirms it is the full-sequence cost.
root_cause: Carryover phrasing from a per-token decode discussion applied to a full-prefill calculation.
correction: Change 'per token per head' to 'per head for the full L-token prefill' (or simply 'per head, for the full sequence').
acceptance_test: The qualifier is consistent with the L²·d_h formula and with the L=9,200 substitution that follows.

quoted_clause: the dominant cost in LLM inference is the arithmetic intensity of transformer matrix multiplications and the memory bandwidth consumed by KV cache reads and writes on every token step
observed: 'Arithmetic intensity' is a ratio (FLOPs/byte), not a cost or a quantity of work. The sentence intends to say that the dominant costs are (a) the compute (FLOPs) of the matrix multiplications and (b) the memory traffic (bytes) of KV reads/writes. Using 'arithmetic intensity' as a noun for the compute cost is imprecise and could confuse a reader who knows the term as a roofline coordinate.
evidence: In the roofline model (Ch 8), arithmetic intensity = FLOPs / bytes. It is the x-axis, not a cost. The 'cost' is the FLOPs (determining compute time) and the bytes (determining memory time).
root_cause: Shorthand that conflates the characteristic (intensity) with the quantity (FLOPs).
correction: Replace 'the arithmetic intensity of transformer matrix multiplications' with 'the FLOP count of transformer matrix multiplications' (or 'the compute demand of the matrix multiplications').
acceptance_test: The sentence names a quantity of work (FLOPs, bytes) rather than a ratio (intensity) as the 'cost.'

quoted_clause: the dominant cost in LLM inference is the arithmetic intensity of transformer matrix multiplications and the memory bandwidth consumed by KV cache reads and writes
observed: Arithmetic intensity is a ratio (FLOPs/byte), not a cost. The sentence conflates a characterization metric with a resource consumption. Memory bandwidth (bytes/s) is a resource consumption; arithmetic intensity is not.
evidence: Arithmetic intensity determines whether compute or bandwidth is the bottleneck; it is a property of the computation, not a cost paid by the system. The actual costs are compute throughput (FLOP/s consumed) and memory bandwidth (bytes/s consumed).
root_cause: Imprecise introductory sentence that treats a ratio as a cost.
correction: Rewrite as 'the dominant costs are the compute required by transformer matrix multiplications and the memory bandwidth consumed by KV cache reads and writes, with arithmetic intensity determining which resource binds.'
acceptance_test: The sentence distinguishes between costs (resources consumed) and metrics (ratios that characterize those costs).

quoted_clause: the host is prefill-starved at peak
observed: 'Prefill-starved' most naturally reads as 'starved of prefill' (lacking prefill work), which is the opposite of the intended meaning (lacking prefill capacity).
evidence: The preceding sentences establish that prefill demand (5.15×10¹⁶ FLOP/s) exceeds the host's peak (7.91×10¹⁵ FLOP/s), so the intended meaning is 'starved of prefill capacity.' The word 'starved' in English typically means 'lacking [thing]' where [thing] is what you need — 'prefill' is what the host has too much demand for, not what it lacks.
root_cause: Ambiguous word choice that permits the opposite reading.
correction: Replace with 'the host is short of prefill compute capacity at peak' or 'the host cannot meet the prefill demand at peak'.
acceptance_test: The phrase unambiguously means the host lacks prefill capacity, not prefill work.

page_hint: Ch 15 §3, KV cache memory footprint paragraph
quoted_clause: $L_{\mathrm{exec}}$ = λ × $W_{\mathrm{exec}}$ ≈ 10 × 8.6
observed: Ch 15 uses subscript 'exec' ($W_{\mathrm{exec}}$) while Ch 17 uses 'GPU-exec' ($W_{\mathrm{GPU\text{-}exec}}$) for the same quantity (8.6 s). The notation differs between chapters for the same value.
evidence: Ch 15: $W_{\mathrm{exec}}$ ≈ 8.6 s. Ch 17 five-time-quantities table: $W_{\mathrm{GPU\text{-}exec}}$ ≈ 8.6 s (1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode). Same value, different subscript. Ch 17 explicitly distinguishes GPU-exec from KV-resident, e2e, queue, and tool-held — distinctions not present in Ch 15's simpler notation.
root_cause: Notation not unified across chapters; Ch 15 uses a simpler subscript that Ch 17 later refines without cross-referencing the change.
correction: Either use the same subscript in both chapters, or add a brief note in Ch 15 that $W_{\mathrm{exec}}$ will be refined to $W_{\mathrm{GPU\text{-}exec}}$ in Ch 17's five-time-quantities table.
acceptance_test: The same quantity has the same notation wherever it appears, or the notation change is explicitly noted at the point of change.

page_hint: Ch 15 §4, 'Goodput vs. Batch Size: the Cache Lever'
quoted_clause: Summing all collective durations can overstate exposed cost when operations overlap. Subtracting every overlapped duration can understate cost when communication slows concurrent compute.
observed: This paragraph about collective communication measurement (NCCL/profiler lanes, overlap accounting) is misplaced in a section whose header and preceding content address prefix caching and batching (Fig 15.2). It addresses multi-GPU interconnect measurement, not the section's topic.
evidence: Section header is 'Goodput vs. Batch Size: the Cache Lever'; preceding paragraph discusses Fig 15.2 (prefix caching cuts prefill work; batching raises decode goodput). The collective durations paragraph discusses CPU progress threads, HBM, device links, NICs, and profiler lanes — all multi-GPU communication measurement topics.
root_cause: Paragraph placed in wrong section — likely a measurement observation appended to the nearest measurement-adjacent section.
correction: Move to Ch 17's measurement section (which already discusses cross-host communication and collectives in 'Request traffic and model collectives are different populations') or to a dedicated multi-GPU measurement subsection.
acceptance_test: The paragraph appears in a section whose stated topic matches its content (multi-GPU communication measurement).

quoted_clause: A startup's CTO shows the architect a warrant to buy two 8×H100 servers
observed: 'Warrant' in this context is nonstandard. The intended meaning is 'authorization,' 'approval,' or 'proposal to proceed.' 'Warrant' more commonly means a legal document (arrest warrant, search warrant) or a financial instrument (warrant to purchase stock). A reader may pause to disambiguate.
evidence: Standard usage: 'warrant' as a noun for a purchase authorization is not found in common technical or business English. 'Proposal,' 'authorization,' or 'plan' would be unambiguous.
root_cause: Word-choice slip.
correction: Replace 'a warrant to buy' with 'a proposal to buy' or 'authorization to buy.'
acceptance_test: The sentence reads without the reader needing to disambiguate the word 'warrant.'

page_hint: Ch 16, Section 8 (Mini-Case), paragraph beginning 'The honest number:'
quoted_clause: capex ~$11.6K + power ~$2.2K for two hosts leaves ≤ ~$26K for staff — upkeep is the power line already counted, so ~$0.2K of the $26.2K remainder is unallocated
observed: The arithmetic gives 40,000 − 11,667 − 2,221 = 26,112, which rounds to $26.1K, not $26.2K. The text then says '$26.2K remainder' and '$0.2K unallocated' (26,200 − 26,000 = 200). The $100 discrepancy (26,112 vs 26,200) is within the '~' tolerance, but the internal subtraction (26.2 − 26.0 = 0.2) is only consistent if the remainder is exactly 26.2K. A reader who recomputes 40 − 11.67 − 2.22 = 26.11 will see a $0.1K gap, not $0.2K.
root_cause: Rounding the remainder up to $26.2K to make the '$0.2K unallocated' arithmetic clean, at the cost of a small inconsistency with the component figures.
correction: Either (a) change '$26.2K remainder' to '$26.1K remainder' and '$0.2K unallocated' to '$0.1K unallocated', or (b) keep the current wording but add '≈' before $26.2K to signal the rounding. Option (a) is cleaner.
acceptance_test: A reader who subtracts 11.67 + 2.22 from 40.00 gets a number consistent with the stated remainder and unallocated amount.

quoted_clause: H_cloud,month = paid host-hours (an occupancy INPUT, supplied or assumed)
observed: This displayed equation is a tautology (H = H). It serves as a placeholder to emphasize that paid host-hours is an input, but it is not a meaningful equation.
evidence: The next displayed equation provides the actual integral form: H_cloud,month = ∫₀ᵀ N_required(t) dt + warm/startup pool + capacity-reservation. The first 'equation' adds no information beyond restating the variable name.
root_cause: Placeholder presented as a displayed equation.
correction: Remove the tautological equation and state in prose that paid host-hours is an input (e.g., 'The paid host-hours H_cloud,month is an occupancy INPUT, supplied or assumed — not derived in this chapter'), then present only the integral form.
acceptance_test: No tautological equation appears; the input nature of paid host-hours is stated in prose or as a labeled definition.

quoted_clause: the FP8 KV screen is ⌈344/35.0⌉ = 10 at peak (11 at the 95% scheduling factor)
observed: '95% scheduling factor' implies only ρ = 0.95 is applied (ρ-only screen), not the full u × ρ policy. The phrasing could be confused with the full provisioning policy which would give 15.
evidence: ⌈344/(35 × 0.95)⌉ = 11 (ρ-only). ⌈344/(35 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = 15 (full u × ρ policy). The text says 11, confirming ρ-only, but the phrase '95% scheduling factor' does not specify that u = 1.
root_cause: Phrasing does not specify which provisioning factors are applied.
correction: Change to '11 at the ρ-only screen (ρ = 0.95, u = 1)' or '11 with only the 95% scheduling factor applied (not the full u × ρ policy).'
acceptance_test: The reader can determine from the phrasing alone which provisioning factors are applied.

page_hint: Ch 17, §17.3 Worked Example, first paragraph of 'Viability at peak'
quoted_clause: the canonical ~8.6 s per-request service time (1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode)
observed: The 1.08 s prefill figure is used as a canonical value throughout the chapter but is not derived in this chunk. A linear-only FLOP calculation (2 × 70e9 × 9,200 / (8 × 989e12 × 0.35)) gives ≈ 0.465 s, not 1.08 s. The 1.08 s is roughly 2.3× the linear-only FLOP time, suggesting it includes attention FLOPs, a lower effective MFU for the memory-bound portions of prefill, or a different convention established in Chapter 8.
evidence: 2 × 70e9 × 9,200 = 1.288e15 FLOP. 8 × 989e12 × 0.35 = 2.7692e15 FLOP/s. 1.288e15 / 2.7692e15 = 0.465 s. The text's 1.08 s is 2.32× this value. The text references 'Chapter 8' for the 35% MFU but does not show the derivation of 1.08 s in this chapter.
root_cause: Cross-chapter dependency: the 1.08 s is a canonical value from an earlier chapter. Within this chunk it is used consistently, but a reader encountering Ch 17 before re-reading Ch 8 may not be able to verify the prefill time independently.
correction: Add a one-line derivation or explicit cross-reference in the first use: e.g., '1.08 s prefill (Ch 8, §8.x: 9,200 tokens at the 35%-MFU effective prefill rate of ~8,500 tok/s, which includes the attention and memory-bound portions beyond the linear-only FLOP floor of 0.47 s).' Alternatively, if the 1.08 s comes from a different MFU or FLOP convention, state that explicitly so the reader can trace the number.
acceptance_test: A reader who has not read Ch 8 can trace the 1.08 s to a stated rate or formula in this chapter or a precise section reference, and the number is consistent with the 35% MFU and 8×H100 hardware stated elsewhere in the chapter.

quoted_clause: kernel-mode preemption, memory fragmentation, and concurrent kernel launches can increase per-token latency by 20–50%
observed: The 20–50% range is presented as a general engineering observation without an evidence label. It is plausible but not sourced to a measurement, paper, or vendor document. The adjacent recommendation ('add a 20% safety margin') is a design heuristic that should be clearly marked as such.
evidence: No citation, no [ILLUSTRATIVE] or [ASSUMPTION] label, no 'typically' or 'in our experience' qualifier that would mark it as an engineering judgment rather than a measured fact.
root_cause: The claim is a reasonable rule of thumb but is stated with the same authority as the derived arithmetic elsewhere in the chapter.
correction: Add a label: 'can increase per-token latency by 20–50% [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] — a planning heuristic; measure the actual tail inflation on the target workload (Ch 14) before sizing the safety margin.' This preserves the practical guidance while making the epistemic status explicit.
acceptance_test: The 20–50% figure carries an evidence label consistent with the book's three-axis taxonomy, and the 20% margin is framed as a starting heuristic to be replaced by measurement.

page_hint: Ch 17, §17.6 Architecture Consequence, 'Failover and redundancy' paragraph
quoted_clause: Health-check frequency and graceful drain procedures affect the real-world failover time, typically 5–15 seconds
observed: The 5–15 s range is stated without an evidence label or source. It is a reasonable engineering estimate for software-based LB failover but is presented as a general fact.
evidence: No [ILLUSTRATIVE] or [ASSUMPTION] label. No reference to a specific LB product's documented failover time.
root_cause: The figure is a planning heuristic, not a measured or specified value.
correction: Add: 'typically 5–15 seconds [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] for software LBs with 2–5 s health-check intervals; verify against the specific LB product's documented failover and drain times before sizing the N−1 reserve.'
acceptance_test: The 5–15 s figure carries an evidence label and is scoped to a specific LB configuration class.

quoted_clause: the same demand ÷ ceiling written in PFLOP/s, 2 × 1.5099 ÷ 2.7692
observed: The notation '2 × 1.5099 ÷ 2.7692' is arithmetically correct (2 req/s × 1.5099 PFLOP/req ÷ 2.7692 PFLOP/s = 1.0905 ≈ 109%) but the leading '2' can be misread as the '2×' in the FLOP-per-token formula (2 × N) rather than the 2 req/s arrival rate. A reader scanning quickly might parse it as '2 × 1.5099' meaning 'twice 1.5099 PFLOP' rather than '2 requests per second times 1.5099 PFLOP per request.'
evidence: 2 × 1.5099 = 3.0198 PFLOP/s demand. 3.0198 / 2.7692 = 1.0905. The arithmetic is correct. The ambiguity is in the notation, not the number.
root_cause: The '2' serves double duty as both a rate (2 req/s) and a familiar multiplier in FLOP formulas (2 × N × tokens).
correction: Reword to: 'the same ratio in PFLOP/s: (2 req/s × 1.5099 PFLOP/req) ÷ 2.7692 PFLOP/s = 3.02 ÷ 2.77 ≈ 109%.' Adding units to each factor removes the ambiguity.
acceptance_test: A reader can parse each factor's unit (req/s, PFLOP/req, PFLOP/s) without re-reading the surrounding paragraph.

quoted_clause: This reduces cross-host communication but limits the effective parallelism, because a popular user can pin a single host to capacity while other hosts stand underutilized
observed: The text correctly identifies the session-affinity trade-off but does not connect it back to the provisioning formula. The ρ factor in Table 17-1 captures 'load-balancer / scheduling efficiency' including 'affinity skew,' but the reader must infer that a high-affinity workload (e.g., 80% of traffic from 10% of users) would lower ρ below 0.95 and increase the host count. The Common Mistakes section (#2) mentions the Gini coefficient but does not show the arithmetic connection to ρ.
evidence: Table 17-1 defines ρ = 0.95 as the canonical value. The session-affinity paragraph describes the mechanism but does not quantify its effect on ρ or N. The Gini discussion in Common Mistakes #2 says 'the trigger to abandon sticky sessions depends on the workload' but does not show how a measured Gini of, say, 0.5 would change ρ from 0.95 to, e.g., 0.85, and how that changes N from 31 to ⌈344/(17×0.70×0.85)⌉ = ⌈344/10.115⌉ = 35.
root_cause: The session-affinity discussion and the provisioning formula are in different sections (§17.2 vs §17.4) and the connection is left to the reader.
correction: Add one sentence at the end of the session-affinity paragraph: 'In the provisioning formula (Table 17-1), affinity skew enters through ρ: a workload where a few users dominate traffic may push ρ below the 0.95 canonical value, increasing N proportionally (e.g., ρ = 0.85 raises the 31-host policy count to ⌈344/(17×0.70×0.85)⌉ = 35). Measure the per-host load distribution before fixing ρ.'
acceptance_test: A reader can trace from the session-affinity discussion to a specific change in the provisioning formula's ρ parameter and the resulting host count.

quoted_clause: ~2.0 req/s (Ch. 17/20) is the KV-slot-based analytical UPPER bound on admitted request completion rate, conditional on an assumed mean KV residency time (C ÷ E[W_KV-resident])
observed: The reconciliation box is a critical piece of the chapter that prevents confusion between four different 'throughput' numbers. However, it is a single dense paragraph of ~200 words with four numbered items, a decomposition, a warning, and a scope note. The cognitive load is high for a first reading. The box's most important message — 'Do not set a summed 19K tok/s against any single-phase capacity' — is buried in the middle of the paragraph.
evidence: The box contains: (1) four rate definitions, (2) a 'do not sum' warning, (3) a decomposition of 2.0 req/s into 18,400 + 600 tok/s, (4) a 'numerical coincidence' clarification, (5) a scope note about phase-resolved comparison, (6) a [DERIVED] label. All in one paragraph with no sub-structure.
root_cause: The box tries to do too much in one block: define, warn, decompose, clarify, and scope. The reader must hold all six elements in working memory simultaneously.
correction: Break the box into two or three shorter blocks with sub-headings: (a) 'The four rates' (items 1–4), (b) 'The decomposition and the coincidence' (the 18,400 + 600 split and the 'numerical coincidence' paragraph), (c) 'The rule' (the 'Do not set a summed…' warning and the phase-resolved comparison instruction). This preserves all content while reducing the per-block cognitive load. Alternatively, move the 'numerical coincidence' clarification to a footnote and keep the main box focused on the four definitions and the decomposition rule.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify the box's single most important instruction ('do not sum across phases') within 5 seconds of scanning, without reading the full 200-word paragraph.

page_hint: Ch 17, §17.3 and §17.4, the '17.51 cannot round up' phrase
quoted_clause: the conservative integer 'requests that fit' floor is 17, not 18 — 17.51 cannot round up for a hard fit
observed: This exact clarification appears twice: once in §17.3 (Worked Example) and once in §17.4 (Measurement, per-host throughput). The second occurrence is in a different context (the T=0 row of the C calculation list) but the wording is nearly identical. While the first occurrence is necessary (it introduces the floor concept), the second is a local reminder that adds no new information.
evidence: §17.3: 'C = 436 GB ÷ 24.9037 GB ≈ 17.5 concurrent requests (byte-accurate; the conservative integer "requests that fit" floor is 17, not 18 — 17.51 cannot round up for a hard fit).' §17.4: 'C = 436 GB / (9,500 ×2.62 MB) ≈ 436/24.9037 ≈ 17.5 concurrent requests per host (byte-accurate; the conservative integer "requests that fit" floor is 17, not 18 — 17.51 cannot round up for a hard fit).'
root_cause: The §17.4 list re-derives the T=0 case that was already shown in §17.3. The floor clarification is repeated verbatim.
correction: In §17.4, shorten the T=0 entry to: 'C = 436 / 24.9037 ≈ 17.5 → floor 17 (see §17.3 for the rounding rule).' This preserves the number without repeating the full explanation.
acceptance_test: The floor rule is stated in full once and referenced (not repeated) the second time.

quoted_clause: a well-configured software LB (NGINX) typically achieves ρ ≈ 0.95, and a hardware L7 switch may achieve ρ ≈ 0.98
observed: The ρ values for NGINX (0.95) and hardware L7 (0.98) are labeled [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] in the surrounding text, which is correct. However, the specific product names (NGINX, HAProxy, Cloud Load Balancer, F5) appear in both §17.2 and §17.6 without a time-sensitivity note. LB product capabilities and configurations change; a reader in 2028 may find that the specific products or their typical ρ values have shifted. The [ILLUSTRATIVE] label covers the numbers but not the product names.
evidence: The text says 'These LB-efficiency values are [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] engineering thresholds, not universal vendor-independent constants' which correctly scopes the numbers. But the product names are presented as current examples without a date or 'as of' qualifier.
root_cause: Product names in a rapidly evolving field age quickly. The numbers are appropriately labeled, but the product associations are not.
correction: Add a brief time-sensitivity note: 'Product names (NGINX, HAProxy, F5, Cloud LB) are illustrative as of the 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff; the ρ values are engineering thresholds to be measured on the specific product and topology in use, not vendor specifications.' This is consistent with the book's time-sensitivity policy.
acceptance_test: The product names carry a date or 'as of' qualifier, and the text makes clear that the ρ values are not vendor specifications but engineering thresholds to be measured.

quoted_clause: typically ρ ∈ [0.85, 0.98] depending on LB sophistication
observed: The lower bound 0.85 is never explained or justified anywhere in the chapter. The measurement section (§17.4) only discusses ρ ≈ 0.95 (software LB) and ρ ≈ 0.98 (hardware L7 switch).
evidence: §17.4 states 'a well‑configured software LB (NGINX) typically achieves ρ ≈ 0.95, and a hardware L7 switch may achieve ρ ≈ 0.98' — no mention of 0.85. Table 17-1 canonical value is 0.95.
root_cause: Range in mental model not reconciled with the values discussed in the measurement section.
correction: Either explain what configuration yields ρ ≈ 0.85 (e.g., poorly-configured LB, high health-check overhead), narrow the range to [0.95, 0.98] to match §17.4, or add a brief note that 0.85 represents a degraded configuration.
acceptance_test: The lower bound of the ρ range is explained, or the range matches the values discussed in §17.4.

quoted_clause: Every one of 29/32/34/82/205/410 (no-reuse FP8 in the agentic columns)
observed: The parenthetical describes 82/205/410 as 'no-reuse FP8' but those are FP16 no-reuse values per the table row 'N @ T=3, FP16 no-reuse (C=13; 8.645)'. FP8 no-reuse values are 40/99/198.
evidence: Table 17-2 row 'N @ T=3, FP16 no-reuse' gives 82/205/410; row 'N @ T=3, FP8 no-reuse' gives 40/99/198. The parenthetical's precision label does not match the row that produced the listed numbers.
root_cause: Parenthetical mislabels FP16 values as FP8.
correction: Change '(no-reuse FP8 in the agentic columns)' to '(no-reuse FP16 in the agentic columns)', or list the FP8 no-reuse values (40/99/198) as a separate item in the sentence.
acceptance_test: The parenthetical's precision label matches the table row that produced the listed numbers.
